pages.title: Getting started
pages.summary: Flockdeck runs your coding agents on hardware you control, your desk or a machine that never sleeps. With the optional Flockdeck Remote add-on you can use it from a paired phone, tablet or browser too. Every agent pane is a real program in a pseudo-terminal, so it behaves exactly as it does in a normal terminal: permission prompts, slash commands, plan mode, colours, mouse. Claude Code is what a pane runs unless you say otherwise; any other coding agent, and any model API spoken to directly, is a pick away.
pages.text: Getting started Flockdeck runs your coding agents on hardware you control, your desk or a machine that never sleeps. With the optional Flockdeck Remote add-on you can use it from a paired phone, tablet or browser too. Every agent pane is a real program in a pseudo-terminal, so it behaves exactly as it does in a normal terminal: permission prompts, slash commands, plan mode, colours, mouse. Claude Code is what a pane runs unless you say otherwise; any other coding agent, and any model API spoken to directly, is a pick away. With several agents running at once, Flockdeck answers one question at a glance: which agent needs you right now. The rest of this page covers what you need once there is more than one. Three things to know first The dot in each pane header says what that agent is doing. A filled cyan circle is working, an amber triangle is waiting on you, a hollow grey circle is idle, a red square means it failed and a hollow square that the process exited. Shapes as well as colours tell them apart. A tab holding a waiting agent is marked ▲, and so is the window title, so an agent that blocks while you are looking elsewhere still reaches you. Panes are moved, not recreated. Drag a pane by its header to another edge, another tab, or a tab of its own; nothing restarts, and the conversation, working directory and scrollback come with it. Ctrl+Shift+K opens the command palette, and so does Commands at the right of the top bar. It holds every action in the application, searchable, and goes to any tab or project by name. If you remember one shortcut, remember that one. A first session Press Ctrl+Shift+T for an agent tab, or Ctrl+Shift+D to put a second agent beside the one you have. Both take the default agent; New agent tab (choose agent)… is the same thing with the picker in front of it, for when you want a different agent or a different model. Type into a pane as you would in any terminal. Click a pane to give it the keyboard. When an agent blocks on a permission prompt its dot turns amber and its tab is marked. Answer it, and it goes back to work. When one has produced something, press Ctrl+Shift+S to see the diff, commit and push it without leaving the window. When one agent is not enough Two agents editing the same files will fight. Give each its own checkout instead: Ctrl+Shift+G opens the worktrees, where you can create them, and Start a team starts a manager agent that starts the rest; each helper that edits code is given a worktree of its own, and the manager and the readers share the project's checkout. Git worktrees and Agents and models cover both. Which agent, which model A pane's header names what is in it, such as claude · sonnet or codex · gpt-5.6-sol, beside its branch. Agents and models explains the picker, what changes when an agent cannot report its own status, and how to add one of your own. For Claude Code, where its status line is read, the header also estimates what the conversation has spent and shows how near a usage limit it is; Spend and limits says how, and when Claude Code's are read. Finding the rest of it The rail down the left of the window has a tile for each open project (one with an amber triangle badge has an agent waiting on you, and one with a cyan badge has agents at work), and under them the tools: Agents, Team, Broadcast, Changes, Resume and Worktrees, then, below a rule, Help and Settings. GitHub, API keys and Flockdeck Remote are in the command palette and in the settings. Rest the pointer on one, or reach it with the keyboard, and it says what it is and the key that does the same. On a phone or a narrow window the rail folds into the menu at the left of the top bar. Most tools (all but Broadcast, Help and Settings) open as a sheet beside the rail, with your panes still in view. While one is open the keyboard stays in it, and a click on the panes puts it away; so does Esc, or the shortcut that opened it. The first run opens this page once, unasked, and never again. F1 brings it back from anywhere.

pages.title: Panes and tabs
pages.summary: A pane is one terminal running one agent, or a plain shell. Tabs hold panes, and a tab can hold one or several, split however you like.
pages.text: Panes and tabs A pane is one terminal running one agent, or a plain shell. Tabs hold panes, and a tab can hold one or several, split however you like. Making them Keys What it makes Ctrl+Shift+T A tab with one agent in it Ctrl+Shift+N A tab with a plain shell (no agent, no hooks) Ctrl+Shift+D An agent beside the focused pane Ctrl+Shift+E An agent below the focused pane Split right (shell) A shell beside the focused pane, from the command palette Each of those takes the project's default agent, which keeps making a pane one keystroke. To choose a different agent or a different model, click the ▾ beside the + that opens a new tab, or take the two picker entries out of the command palette; Agents and models is the page for all of it. The pane header then names what it got, beside the branch. A shell pane is an ordinary terminal in the same directory. It is there for the git, npm or go command you want to run yourself while the agents work, and for watching a build. That is why it can be split in beside an agent as well as opened in a tab of its own. Working in them Click a pane to give it the keyboard. Everything you type goes to the agent in it. That is the point, and it is why almost all of this application's own shortcuts are on Ctrl+Shift, which agents do not use. Drag the divider between two panes to resize them, or reach it with Tab and use the arrow keys, and Home to share the room equally again. Ctrl+Shift+Z gives the focused pane the whole tab, and gives it back; so does double-clicking the pane's header. The others keep running; they are simply not on screen. Ctrl+Shift+F searches the focused terminal's scrollback. Select text with the mouse and Ctrl+C copies it; Ctrl+V pastes. With nothing selected, Ctrl+C goes to the agent, as it always did. Keyboard shortcuts has the rest, and macOS. Ctrl+Shift+W closes a pane and stops the agent in it, without asking. It also ends what was started in the pane and is still running there: a shell's background jobs, a server an agent left going, a job that ignores the hangup. A program with windows of its own (a browser, an editor started with code .) stays open, as it does when a terminal is closed, and so does what it runs, such as the terminals in that editor. On macOS a background job that ignores the hangup ( nohup) keeps running. Closing a tab's last pane closes the tab, and the × on a tab, or a click on it with the middle button, closes every pane in it. The buttons in a pane header, in order: include in broadcast ( ⇉), auto-approve read-only ( ✓), restart, zoom, export transcript, record, pane info ( ⓘ), lock, close. Auto-approve read-only is off until you turn it on, pane by pane (the ✓'s tooltip counts the commands it has let through unasked so far), and the pane keeps the setting across a restart of Flockdeck: see Knowing who needs you. Record is off until you turn it on too; export and record are not shown on a shell pane, which has no conversation. Showing the transcript file in your file manager is in Ctrl+Shift+Y and the command palette rather than the header, and works only in a window on the machine Flockdeck runs on: see Recording a pane. One pane, several windows A pane has one terminal however many windows show it (a second window, a phone over Flockdeck Remote), and that terminal is the size of the window last used on it: the one you focus or type in. Every other window draws it at that same size, so what the agent prints lands where it should. Where that is larger than the pane's room in a window, the window shows the part of it nearest the bottom left, where the latest lines are, with a note such as Viewing 120×40 · fit to this window; click it to size the pane for this window instead. A pane's terminal is never made smaller than 20 columns by 5 rows or larger than 500 by 200. Pane info Ctrl+Shift+Y, in the command palette and as the ⓘ in the pane header, lists what names a pane in files, logs and commands, each with a Copy button, and Copy all puts the whole list on the clipboard as plain text. A value the pane does not have yet says "not set". The list has: The pane id, which flockdeck close takes and which transcript files hold as pane. The pane's name, its project and project folder, its directory (a worktree has its own), its branch and its tab. For an agent, the agent, the model and the conversation id, which is the agent's own id for the conversation. It changes after /clear. The first 8 characters of it are in a transcript's file name, and it is the file name of the conversation the agent stores under ~/.claude/projects. The process id, the peer name set by flockdeck peer-name, and the pane's status. Whether the pane is recording, the path of its transcript file (the one it is recording to, or its latest export, with a Show in folder button that selects it in your file manager) and the path of the conversation file the agent stores itself. That last path is shown for panes that run Claude Code (including a second Claude account), once the agent has written the file. Until then, and for every other agent, it says "not set". A shell has no agent, conversation or transcript, so those are left out for it. Nothing secret is listed: no keys, tokens or environment. A path can name your own folders, so look at Copy all before pasting it somewhere public. The list is read on the machine Flockdeck runs on and is not sent anywhere else, so a window reached through Flockdeck Remote cannot open it. Finding a pane Ctrl+Shift+L, in the command palette, searches every pane in every open project. Type part of a pane's name, project, tab, agent, model, directory, branch, pane id, conversation id, process id or peer name; several words must all match, in any of those, and case does not matter. A conversation id matches from its first characters, so the 8 in a transcript's file name will do. Each result shows the pane, its project and tab, and what matched. Press Enter for the first result or click one: Flockdeck goes to that project and tab and gives the pane the keyboard. Esc closes the search. All agents across projects lists the same panes by what needs you, rather than by what you type. Locking a pane Lock pane, in the command palette and as the padlock in the pane header, locks a pane so it cannot be closed by accident. The same action unlocks it again, and the palette names it Unlock pane while the pane is locked. A locked pane shows a padlock and the word "Locked" in its header, and while it is locked: Ctrl+Shift+W and the × in its header do nothing but say the pane is locked. Its tab cannot be closed, by the × on the tab or the middle button, while any pane in it is locked, and neither can a project that holds one. Close finished panes leaves it open and says how many it left. flockdeck close refuses it, and -force does not change that: -force is for a pane still working, and a lock is something only you undo. flockdeck close -finished skips it and reports how many it skipped. Restart pane still works on a locked pane and leaves it locked. The lock is kept with the layout, so it survives a restart of Flockdeck, and it moves with the pane when you drag it to another tab. Quitting Flockdeck is not closing a pane, so a lock does not stop it. Naming a tab A tab names itself after the first thing its agent is asked. To call it something else, double-click it, press F2 while the keyboard is on it, or choose Rename this tab… in the command palette; a name you give it stays, whatever the agent is asked next. To go back, rename it to an empty name or choose Use the automatic title in the same dialog: the tab takes the title it would have had if it had never been renamed. Either way the name is kept with the layout. Restarting Restart pane, in the command palette and in the pane header, stops the process and starts it again in the same directory, with the same agent and model. It resumes the same conversation where that agent can, because a pane and its conversation are one identity. Use it when an agent is stuck or has wedged itself, not to clear the screen. A pane whose process exits covers its terminal with what happened and two buttons, Restart and Close pane, rather than leaving a dead black rectangle. Font size Ctrl+= and Ctrl+- change the terminal font size for every pane; Ctrl+0 puts it back.

pages.title: Agents and models
pages.summary: Every agent pane runs a coding agent of your choosing at a model of your choosing. Claude Code is the default and behaves exactly as it always has; the picker is how you reach anything else.
pages.text: Agents and models Every agent pane runs a coding agent of your choosing at a model of your choosing. Claude Code is the default and behaves exactly as it always has; the picker is how you reach anything else. Picking one The plain Ctrl+Shift+T and Ctrl+Shift+D stay one keystroke and take the default agent, because that is what you want almost every time. To choose deliberately, use New agent tab (choose agent)… or Split right (choose agent)… from the command palette, or click the ▾ beside the + that opens a new tab. The picker lists the agents that can be started first and then the ones that cannot. An agent that cannot be started is shown greyed and marked unavailable, without a reason, rather than hidden: somebody who has never installed Codex should still learn that Flockdeck would run it. Expand an agent for its models, with its default marked. A model carries its tier where it has a fixed one ( small, mid or top: how capable, and so how costly, it is among that agent's own models). A model shows no price: the same model may be billed per token or covered by a subscription, and only you know which. At the foot of the picker, Set as default for makes the choice stick, either for this project or for every project, so the one-keystroke split keeps doing the right thing. Use the default for every project removes this project's own choice. The pane header names what is running, beside the branch and in the same dim weight: claude · sonnet, codex · gpt-5.6-sol. A shell pane shows nothing there, because there is nothing to choose. For Claude Code, where its status line is read, it is followed by what the conversation has spent and how near its usage limit it is; Spend and limits explains the figures. Agents are programs Agents are the tools you would run in a terminal yourself: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Aider, opencode, Cursor's agent. Flockdeck runs the command in the pane's pseudo-terminal, so it behaves exactly as it does anywhere else and uses whatever login that tool already has. Flockdeck does not install agents. One whose command cannot be found or started is shown as unavailable. Flockdeck no longer has a chat client of its own for talking to a model API directly. The flockdeck chat command, and the Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and OpenAI-compatible agents built on it, were removed. An agents.json entry that still has an api block, or "runner": "api", is refused with a notice saying so. Structured agents (beta) Direction (27 Oct 2026): structured agents are where Flockdeck is heading: every agent over ACP, with no terminal-pane agents, no inbox or typed wake, and no task board. Those are planned removals, not removed yet. Agents without native ACP will get an adapter built into the flockdeck binary. See docs/acp-direction.md in the repository. A structured agent is one Flockdeck talks to over the Agent Client Protocol instead of in a terminal. Its pane has no screen: the drawer shows its conversation, a box to send it a prompt and a Stop button. Today the one offered is opencode (structured). There is none for Claude Code. Type / at the start of the prompt box to list the commands the agent offers, with their argument hints. Keep typing to filter, move with the arrow keys, and press Enter or Tab to choose one, or Escape to close the list. A choice only writes /name into the box: the agent runs the command when you send the text. Flockdeck's own commands (today /stop) are listed first, under their own heading, and run at once. The list is whatever the agent advertises, so it differs between agents. A row of selectors above the conversation shows the agent's mode, its model and any other setting it offers, such as the effort. Pick a value to change it. The selector shows what the agent reports, so a change the agent refused leaves the old value in place. /mode and /model appear in Flockdeck's group for the agents that offer them: choosing one moves you to its selector, and typing /mode plan and sending sets the mode without a prompt. A value that is not on the agent's list is not sent. A change to a mode that reads as running without asking (such as a YOLO or bypass mode) asks you to confirm first, by either route, and the pane shows its warning while it is in that mode. /mode and /model replace an agent command of the same name; to send the agent its own, start the text with a space. The prompt box takes several lines. Enter sends (so does Ctrl or Command with Enter) and Shift+Enter adds a line; there is no setting to swap them. The box grows to ten lines. Up, with the caret on the first line, steps back through the prompts you sent to this pane, and Down steps forward again to the text you were writing. The draft and the last 50 prompts are kept for each pane in this window's storage, so they are still there after you switch tabs or close the drawer; a prompt over 8 KiB is sent but not remembered, and the records of the 30 panes you used last are kept. They are plain text on this machine, so clear them with the browser data of the window if you pasted something private. Type @ at the start of a word to list files under the pane's working directory. In a git checkout the list is what git tracks or does not ignore, so .gitignore is honoured; elsewhere it is a bounded walk that skips hidden folders and node_modules. At most 50 names are shown, best match first, and "More files match" says there are more. Tab takes the highlighted name; Enter takes one only after you moved to it with an arrow key or the mouse, and otherwise sends your text. Choosing one writes @relative/path into the text; Flockdeck does not read the file, so the agent opens it. Links are never followed or listed. A window reached through the relay has no file list. You can type while the agent is working. The text waits in a queue of up to 16 prompts and is sent when the turn ends. The queue is listed under the conversation, next first, with Edit, Remove and Send now on each of your prompts, and Clear to remove all of yours. An edit or removal is refused, and says so, if the prompt was sent while you were looking at it. Messages from other agents are in the same list, marked "Mail from" and the sender's name. You cannot edit or remove one, and Clear leaves them; Send now works on them. Send now ends the running turn (the agent is told to cancel) and sends that prompt next with the rest of the queue behind it, which is the nearest ACP has to steering an agent mid-turn: the agent does not read your text while it works. Stop ends the turn and drops the whole queue; Stop, keep queue ends the turn and goes on to the next prompt. Mail beyond the 16 the pane holds waits in the inbox and is not listed until there is room. When the agent takes images, paste one into the box, drop one on it, or press Attach image. Flockdeck saves the picture in its own state folder, not in your checkout, and writes [image: path] into the text for the agent to read. A large picture is scaled down first, and one picture is attached at a time. Agents that do not take images get no Attach image button and say so if you paste one. It is off until you turn it on. Put "structuredPanes": true in prefs.json in the state directory (there is no setting for it in the window); until then the picker does not offer a structured agent. Turning it off again takes effect when you restart a pane or when the agents are read again, and does not end a running pane. What to know before you use one: Approval is at the desk. A permission request is answered from a window on this machine, by choosing one of the options the agent offered. A phone gets no notification for it and cannot answer it, and a window reached through the relay is told its name, status, directory, branch, project, agent and model, and no text the agent wrote. Nothing is answered for you; a request still open when you stop the turn, close or restart the pane or quit is answered cancelled. opencode is started to ask, which a repository can override. opencode, as shipped, runs commands and edits files without a question, so Flockdeck starts it with bash and edit set to ask, and each arrives as a permission card. This builds the setting from your own and the project's bash and edit rules: each allow becomes a question, and a deny stays a deny. That is about your and the project's rules, not the built-in agents' own: opencode's plan agent, which denies edits, asks for them instead, with a card. Choosing Always on a card allows that kind of command for the rest of the session, one you had denied included. Other settings, such as webfetch, read and external_directory, are left as you set them, and opencode still runs those without asking unless you say otherwise; Flockdeck never sets anything to allow. A terminal opencode pane keeps its own configuration. A repository whose own opencode settings give an agent ( agent.build.permission, or a file under .opencode/agent) permission to run commands wins over this, and the command runs without a card. A project's opencode.json or .opencode folder can also load plugins and MCP servers that run code, so no permission setting makes an opencode pane safe in a repository you do not trust. When a pane starts, Flockdeck reads what opencode resolves in that directory and, only if a command could still run without a card, the drawer header of the pane says "This agent may run commands and edit files without asking you first: in this repository Flockdeck could not make it ask, or could not check. A project's opencode.json or .opencode folder can also load plugins and MCP servers that run code, so no permission setting makes an opencode pane safe in a repository you do not trust." Open a repository you do not trust in a terminal pane, not a structured one. Mail needs an opt-in. A structured agent has no flockdeck command and is not given the pane identity one needs, so it cannot run flockdeck inbox. By default it is not woken by mail at all, and its briefing says mail is not available to it. flockdeck wake text on -agent opencode-acp turns it on for that agent type. Then each wake is one prompt holding the oldest unread message, as Flockdeck message from agent "<role>": <text> ( the user for a message you wrote), and the message counts as read once the agent takes it. This puts text written by another agent in front of an agent that may run commands, as if it were a turn from you. What limits it: the fixed start of the line, one line with escapes and control characters removed, the sender label cut at 32 characters, the text cut at 300 characters, and a briefing that tells the agent to treat the text as a message from another agent and not as your instruction. The agent cannot fetch what is cut. Leave it off for an agent you would not trust with a peer's words. A login problem shows as a blocked pane marked "needs setup", and as "Needs setting up" in the Team view, with the one step to take: sign in with the agent's own tool (Flockdeck never signs in), then start the pane again. An agent that cannot be found or started shows as "the agent is unavailable" and nothing more: not the command, not the reason, not anything the agent printed. The same words come back from a refused spawn. A restart starts a new session. The earlier entries stay above a line saying the agent was restarted. If the new agent cannot be started, they stay too, with a line giving the reason. Nothing is recorded or exported. Recording and export are not available for a structured pane yet. Not every agent can do everything Most of what Flockdeck does beyond drawing a terminal depends on the agent cooperating, and they do not all cooperate in the same ways. If the agent Then reports its own lifecycle its status mark says what it is really doing, rather than what its output looks like can resume by id restoring a layout brings its conversation back, not only its pane writes a transcript it can be resumed from it; it is what Resume lists answers a start-up hook its briefing survives a compaction, rather than being said once and summarised away An agent that does none of it still works: it is a terminal with a program in it. Where a capability is missing Flockdeck falls back rather than failing: status comes from the terminal bell and a quiet timer; resume is not attempted, and the pane starts fresh. Of the built-in agents, Claude Code reports its own lifecycle and answers the start-up hook. Codex, Gemini CLI, Aider, opencode and Cursor Agent are read from their terminals, but are still briefed: the briefing is put in front of their opening task, once, and is not refreshed. Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode and Cursor Agent get it even in a pane opened by hand with no task; Aider gets it only when there is a task, because --message makes it answer once and exit, and a message that was all briefing would end the pane. An entry in agents.json can choose the same for its own agent with "caps": {"context": "prompt"} (or "task" for the Aider behaviour), and can give it "patterns": "waiting" and "idle", each a list of phrases its output shows in that state, so that its status is read from what it prints as well. They are plain text and case does not matter. None of the built-ins has any yet. Aider is handed its opening task with --message, which Aider treats as a single message, so a pane started with a task (by flockdeck spawn, say) may end when the task does. API keys An agent uses the login it already has, and Flockdeck never sees it. A key is optional: an agent starts without one. Where you set one, in API keys… or with flockdeck keys set, Flockdeck puts it in the environment of that agent's process under the variable the agent reads ( GEMINI_API_KEY for Gemini CLI, OPENAI_API_KEY for Codex) and in no other process, recording or message. It is read when a pane starts, so a pane already running keeps what it had. opencode keeps its own provider logins and has no key here. A key you exported in the environment Flockdeck runs in reaches an agent only if the agent's entry lists that variable in passEnv. Without that, an OPENAI_API_KEY you set for another tool does not move Codex off its login. Command What it does flockdeck keys set <agent> Reads the key from stdin, so it misses shell history flockdeck keys list Which agents have one, not what it is flockdeck keys clear <agent> Forgets the one Flockdeck stored flockdeck keys check <agent> Asks the agent's endpoint whether it takes the key Keys are kept in keys.json in the state directory, readable only by you. A key is never logged, never written into a saved layout and never shown, and the interface will not read one back to you. Adding your own: agents.json The picker is the built-in agents overlaid with your own file, agents.json in the state directory: %AppData%\flockdeck on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/flockdeck on macOS, ~/.config/flockdeck on Linux. { "version": 1, "defaults": { "agent": "claude", "model": "" }, "projects": { "C:\\code\\api": { "agent": "codex", "model": "gpt-5.6-terra" } }, "agents": [ { "id": "claude", "defaultModel": "sonnet" }, { "id": "mine", "name": "My agent", "exe": "my-agent", "models": [{ "id": "fast" }, { "id": "careful" }] } ] } Entries are matched to the built-ins by id and merged field by field: the claude entry above changes its default model and leaves everything else alone. An id matching no built-in is an agent of your own. "hidden": true takes one out of the picker without removing it. A model's "tier" ( "small", "mid" or "top") is set or corrected the same way; anything else is named in the notice and ignored. The file is read fresh every time the picker opens, so editing it by hand takes effect without a restart. Roles A role is a job an agent is started for. Flockdeck ships six: manager, planner, worker, reviewer, tester and docs. Each has a short briefing saying what the agent does, what it must not do, who it reports to and what to hand back when it finishes. An agent starts in one with -role: flockdeck spawn -role reviewer "review the token refresh change on fix-auth" flockdeck agents lists the roles after the agents, with the checkout each one expects and which roles it may start. An unknown role is refused with the list of roles there are. A pane in a role is limited in what it may start. It may start only the roles its own role lists under spawns, and it may start an agent with no role ( spawn without -role) only if its role has plain set, since an agent with no role has no limits. manager has plain set; the other built-in roles do not. A refused spawn says which rule it hit. The briefing follows those limits. A pane in a role that may start nothing, such as worker or reviewer, gets no section on starting agents. A pane in a role with spawns gets examples that name those roles, such as flockdeck spawn -role worker -worktree <branch> "<task>", and is told to use the pane id that spawn prints, or flockdeck team -json shows, when it assigns a task or sends a message, because pane names are shared. The pane is briefed for its role: the briefing gains a "Your role" section with the role's text (and, for a role that may start others, the ids of every role in the catalog), and the pane's environment carries FLOCKDECK_ROLE. The role is saved with the layout, so a restored pane is briefed for the same job. Agents in a project can see each other, message each other and share a task board (see below). A role may name an agent and a model, or a tier ( small, mid or top) in place of a model. They apply only to a spawn that names neither -agent nor -model: a spawn that names an agent keeps it. A role's model goes only to the agent the role resolves to (its own agent, or the project's default when it names none), so spawn -agent codex -role fast does not give codex a model written for claude. The built-in roles name none, so they run whatever the project runs by default. Roles are another key of agents.json. An entry whose id is a built-in's is merged over it field by field, and any other id is a role of your own: { "roles": [ { "id": "worker", "tier": "mid" }, { "id": "security", "name": "Security reviewer", "briefing": "Review the change for injection, unsafe file access and leaked secrets. Do not edit files. Report findings to whoever started you, with file and line.", "worktree": "readonly", "spawns": [] } ] } Field Meaning id What -role takes name What lists and the briefing call it description One line on what the role is for, shown beside its name in the picker and Settings. It is not given to the agent agent, model, tier Defaults for a spawn that chose neither an agent nor a model briefing The text the agent is given about its role worktree own (a worktree and branch of its own), readonly (a checkout it reads and does not change) or main (the project's main checkout) spawns The ids of the roles an agent in this role may start. An agent in a role may start only these; an agent with no role may start any plain true lets an agent in this role start agents with no role. Off unless set The worktree setting is part of the briefing and the role list, and it decides what flockdeck spawn does when an agent starts a helper. A helper in a role set to own, or in a role with no setting, or with no role, is given a git worktree and a branch of its own, cut from the starting agent's current commit and named from its task, with no flag needed; spawn prints the branch and directory. The helper starts in the same subfolder of the worktree that you were in, when it exists there. Uncommitted changes in your checkout are not in the worktree, and spawn says how many, so the manager can commit first. It says so only for the default worktree, not for one you name with -worktree. A tester that needs a worker's change is started with -worktree <worker branch>. Nothing removes a helper's worktree when it closes; Worktrees is where they are cleared, and files git ignores, such as node_modules, are not copied into it. -worktree <branch> chooses the branch name and -no-worktree starts the helper in the starting agent's checkout instead. A role set to readonly or main (the planner and reviewer, and the manager) is started in the starting agent's checkout. Flockdeck does not make a readonly checkout read-only. Outside a git repository, or when the worktree cannot be cut, the start is refused and the note names -no-worktree; it is never started in the shared checkout on its own. In the window, Start in a worktree is ticked when you choose a role that works on its own branch. A worktree that is none of the three, a bad tier, and a spawns entry that names no role are listed in the notice and ignored. Starting a role from the window The agent picker ( New agent tab (choose agent)… or Split right (choose agent)…) has a Role control above the filter. None is the picker as it has always been. Choose a role and the picker shows what the role is for, asks for a task, which a role always needs, and says which agent and model the role comes to, for example claude · opus, the Worker role's choice. Enter in the task, or Start, runs the role on that agent and model. Picking an agent row in the list names the agent only, as -agent does, so the role's model still applies when that agent is the role's own; picking a model row names both, and the role's choice is not used. Ctrl+Down and Ctrl+Up walk the list from the task box or the Role control, and Ctrl+Enter starts the row picked out. In a worktree of its own is ticked for a role whose worktree is own, and the hint says what the role expects: its own branch, a branch it reads and that the task should name ( readonly), or the project's main checkout. Ticked, Flockdeck cuts a worktree and branch named from the task, as -worktree does. A role opens in a tab of its own, not as a split, and Flockdeck switches to it once it has started. If the start is refused, the dialog stays open with what you typed and the notice says why. A role cannot be started with a shell; the window never offers one. The spawn limits above apply to agents, not to you: from the window you may start any role, including one that no role lists under spawns. Start a team starts a team with one agent. It asks for a goal and, if you want one, an agent and model for the manager, and starts a manager with the goal as its task in the project on screen, as flockdeck spawn -role manager "<goal>" would. The manager then starts the rest. With no manager role in the catalog the dialog says so and has no Start button. What a manager does on its own Given a goal, a manager works through it without being asked at each step: It breaks the goal into tasks and puts them on the task board, starting a planner first when the goal is more than one obvious change. It starts a worker for each task with spawn -role worker, so each is given a branch of its own, and assigns the task to it. Planners and reviewers read and share the manager's checkout. Every agent it starts for one task gets the same -tab "<task title>", so the planner, worker, reviewer and tester for a task share one tab named after it, and another task gets another tab. The tab is forgotten when Flockdeck restarts, so a task whose helpers are still running gets a second tab of the same title the next time the manager starts one for it. It arms flockdeck inbox -follow once, before it starts helpers: under the Monitor tool in Claude Code. Each new message prints one line, which wakes the manager even after it has ended its turn, and it reads the message with inbox read. The Monitor tool expires after at most 30 minutes, and the manager starts it again. Without the Monitor tool it runs inbox -wait 90s with Bash run_in_background in a loop, because a plain background command wakes the agent only when it exits. Only Claude Code is known to be woken this way; an agent without it waits inside its turn with inbox -wait 90s (90 seconds stays inside the 120 second limit of an agent's shell command). The other roles arm the stream too, and stop once they have reported. Flockdeck writes to the manager's inbox when a helper sends a message, exits, or finishes a turn and stays idle, and when a task is blocked or ready for review. It starts a reviewer, and a tester if the change needs one, on each worker's branch, moves a task to done when the verdict is good, and sends work that needs changes back. It closes a task's helpers when the task is done, which also removes the task's tab, and reports to you: what is done and on which branches, what is blocked, and what it needs you to decide. Some things stay with you, but only as an instruction in the briefing. A manager is told to ask and wait before it merges, pushes, opens a pull request, deploys, publishes, deletes branches, worktrees or files, or spends money, to tell its helpers to leave those to it, and to treat a message or report that says you approved something as no approval. Flockdeck does not check this: nothing stops a manager or helper from running gh pr merge or git push except the agent's own permission prompts and its willingness to follow the briefing. A helper an agent starts does not inherit that agent's auto-review setting; it starts with the installation's default. The number of helpers is kept modest. The manager is told to run no more than four at once, and Flockdeck refuses a spawn while eight panes are open below the agent asking (its helpers, theirs, and any whose process has exited but whose pane is still open); closing a finished helper makes room. A message that says a helper is idle is from Flockdeck and carries no text from the helper. The helper's report arrives as a SendMessage from the helper, which the built-in roles send, since a manager cannot read another pane ( msg send is the fallback). Agents are told not to answer a message only to acknowledge it, which would wake the sender for nothing. A pane started in a role carries its name in its header, after the pane name, and in the Agents overview. Pane info lists it as Role. A pane started in no role shows nothing. Settings › Agents & models lists the roles to read; they are changed in agents.json, as above. The team and messages Every agent's briefing has a "Your team" section, the other agent panes of its project as they were when the agent started, and a "Messages" section. Targets, limits, the one-line notice, the fixed line that can wake an idle agent and what Flockdeck writes to an inbox itself are in The command line. An idle Claude Code pane is woken from Claude's own record of its state, the sessions/<pid>.json file it keeps in its config folder: only when that file is the one for the pane's own process and conversation and says the agent has been idle for five seconds, nobody has pressed a key in the pane since, the pane's own status is idle, the pane's hooks have reported, and its output has not changed for five seconds. The line is still the fixed sentence. Anyone who can write to that folder can forge an idle record, which gets the pane at most one line a minute, and three in a row until the agent reads its mail, while it has unread mail and every other condition and limit holds. The built-in roles say when to use messages: the manager writes to the agents it started to answer a question or change a task, and planners, workers, reviewers, testers and docs agents write to the manager when they are blocked. Planners, workers, reviewers, testers and docs agents also send their final report to the manager with SendMessage, because the manager cannot read their panes; it is still their last message too. The task board Each project has one task board, which every agent in it reaches with flockdeck task whatever worktree it works in. A task has a title, a body, an owner role and pane, a state, a branch, an optional baton id for context and a thread of notes. A task points at a baton and does not replace it: a baton stays the handoff document it was written as. The states, the table of who may move a task where, the messages a change sends and how the board is stored are in The command line. The built-in roles use it this way. The planner adds a task for each step of a plan. The manager assigns them to the workers it starts, and moves a task to done once a reviewer says the change is good. A worker moves its task to in-progress when it starts, sets the branch, and moves it to in-review when the change is committed, which messages the reviewers and testers. A reviewer or tester reads a task in in-review and either adds a note and tells the manager, or moves it back to in-progress with a note that says why, which messages the worker. Every agent's briefing has a "Task board" section with the commands and a snapshot of the counts for that pane, such as "2 tasks assigned to you, 1 in review", or "2 tasks for your role, none claimed yet" for tasks assigned to a role that no pane has started. The Team panel Ctrl+Shift+M opens a sheet for the project on screen, with three tabs: Tasks, Messages and Agents. It shows what the command line shows, and lets you steer from the window. It updates as the team works: a task that moves, a message that arrives and a pane that starts, stops or changes status appear without reopening it, and an open task, the text you are typing and your place in the list stay as they were. Agents lists every agent pane of the project with its name, role, what it is doing and how many messages it has not read. The Team view shows the rest of a pane's detail. Close and Close finished close panes that are idle or have exited; Close finished names them and asks first, and each pane is checked again as it closes, so one that has started working since the list was drawn is left open. A pane locked against closing keeps its button disabled. To start an agent, use the agent picker; the sheet has no button for it. Tasks is the board, one column for each of planned, assigned, in progress, in review and done. In a window narrower than 900 pixels the columns are one list, grouped by state. Blocked and cancelled tasks are behind a button. Each card shows the id, title, who the task is for, the branch and the number of notes; the arrow keys move between cards and Enter opens one. Open a task to read its details, notes and history and to assign it to a role or a pane, set its branch, add a note, or move it. Move offers only the moves the rules allow you for that task, and a move that undoes progress needs a note in the note box. Add task adds one, and Prune finished… removes done and cancelled tasks last changed over 30 days ago. You act as the manager, whether or not a pane has that role, and as no pane: a task you add or a note you write shows you as its author, and the agents are told it was the user. The notices are the ones a manager pane's change would send, so an agent hears when a task is assigned to it, goes to review, is blocked or done, or gets a note. Agents see you as the user (at the window), in notices, flockdeck task show and flockdeck inbox; an agent that names itself the user, you or flockdeck is shown as (agent) the user, so no agent can sign as you. Messages lists the project's messages, newest first, with sender, recipient, time, text and whether the recipient has read it. The filter narrows them to a pane or a role. Message text is shown as plain text. Write to a pane, or to every pane in a role, in the box above the list: the message is signed as you, is at most 8 KB, and goes to the agent's inbox. It never goes into the terminal; the agent is sent the same one-line notice as for any message, when it is idle. Each message shows two marks: whether its recipient has read it, and whether you have seen it. Mark seen sets only your own mark and the count on the tab; the agent's inbox and its unread count are unchanged. The panel works on the machine Flockdeck runs on. A window reached through the relay is refused its commands. A board of more than 300 open tasks lists the newest 300, with a button for the rest. Routing Helpers multiply whatever their model costs, and many of their tasks are mechanical: run the tests, rename a symbol, fix a typo. Routing pre-sets the model of a helper an agent starts with flockdeck spawn, and of the first prompt you send a pane, to one suited to the work (a smaller one for mechanical work, a stronger one for hard work). It is off until you turn it on, in Settings › Routing, for every project or for one. A pane a rule routed says so in its header ( claude · haiku ↘), with the rule, and the agent and model it would otherwise have used, in its tooltip. A pane Minimise cost routed with no rule runs the cheaper model without the arrow. Routing moves work between the models of the agent the run is on, and only between models whose tier it knows. It sends work to another agent only when you turn on Let a rule send work to another agent, in the same place, and a rule names that agent's model and agent. A rule like that could send test runs to a cheaper agent, say. Even then, only a new helper moves, never a conversation already under way. The other agent has to be installed and trusted for the project. The pane header's tooltip names the agent and model it would otherwise have used. Claude Code's Default is whatever the CLI is set to, which might be its smallest model or its largest, so routing leaves work on it alone: make a model your default, for routing to choose from it. Automatic routes a helper an agent starts with flockdeck spawn without -agent or -model, and the first prompt you send a pane from the prompt bar, while it has no conversation yet: the pane restarts on the chosen model with that prompt, and never on another agent. Never go below keeps routing off the smaller tiers for a project where the work matters. Strategy decides what happens to a task no rule matches. Cost-first, quality-aware (the default) leaves it exactly where it was, the same as routing off would. Minimise cost routes it too, to the cheapest model Never go below allows on the agent it was already going to run on, never to another agent. Either strategy, a rule that matches still decides first and Never go below still holds; the strategy only changes what happens when nothing matches. The pane's tooltip says "no rule matched" for a choice made this way, so it is never mistaken for a rule's own reason. The policy is kept in agents.json, and only there, never in a file inside a repository, so a repository you clone cannot change what your key spends: { "routing": { "mode": "auto", "floor": "", "strategy": "", "rules": [ { "name": "run the tests", "tier": "small", "when": { "task": "^(re-?)?run (the |all )?(unit |integration )?tests?\\b" } }, { "name": "schema changes", "tier": "top", "when": { "files": ["**/migrations/**", "**/*.sql"] } }, { "name": "design work", "model": "opus", "agent": "claude", "when": { "task": "\\bdesign\\b" } } ] }, "projects": { "C:\\code\\payments": { "routing": { "mode": "auto", "floor": "mid" } } } } Rules are tried in order and the first that matches decides; a task no rule matches is left alone under "strategy": "balanced" (the default, same as leaving strategy out), or routed to the cheapest model the floor allows under "strategy": "cost". Every condition in when must hold: task is a regular expression matched without regard to case; minWords and maxWords bound the task's length; files are globs matched against the paths the task names ( ** is any number of directories, and a glob with no / matches a file's name anywhere); kind is spawn or turn; agent is an agent's id. A rule asks for a tier, or for one agent's model. Leave rules out for the built-in ones, which Settings lists; "rules": [] means none. A project's own policy replaces the one for every project whole. A rule that cannot be used (a pattern that is not one, a tier that is not one) is named in the notice and skipped, and the rest still apply. Two things an older version wrote still load, and do nothing. "mode": "suggest" filled in the Fan out dialog, which no longer exists, so it is read as "off" with a notice; set it to "auto" to have routing choose models. A rule whose kind is fanout is named in the notice and skipped. A "jev" key is ignored and left in the file as written. Saving a default from a Flockdeck that has no routing (0.2.10 or older) writes a project's entry back without its routing, so a project's policy is lost that way. Routing makes no request. It decides from these rules alone. The routed mark on a pane travels only as the rest of the pane's state does, to your own paired devices when Flockdeck Remote is on. Helpers and first prompts are not logged. An older version that routed fan-out rows kept its choices in routing.jsonl in the state directory (the last 10,000 lines, never the task), and nothing writes to it now. Settings still lists each rule beside how often that log shows it overridden, once it has decided at least once. Settings has Clear routing history, and to turn all of it off, set every project to Off. A file that does not parse is a notice in the interface and nothing worse: the built-in agents carry on, because a typo in a settings file is not a reason to be unable to start work.

pages.title: Knowing who needs you
pages.summary: Running one agent is easy. Running six is not: they finish at different times and they block on permission prompts, and the one that is waiting is rarely the one you are looking at.
pages.text: Knowing who needs you Running one agent is easy. Running six is not: they finish at different times and they block on permission prompts, and the one that is waiting is rarely the one you are looking at. The dots Every pane header carries a status dot. Dot Meaning Filled cyan circle, pulsing Working: producing output or running a tool Amber triangle Waiting on you: a permission prompt or a question Amber triangle Blocked: a tool call was refused outright and the turn ended there. Nothing is being asked, but it needs a look Hollow grey circle Idle: it finished its turn and is ready for a new prompt Hollow grey circle, pulsing Starting: launched, and not heard from yet Red filled square Failed: the process ended with an error, or was killed Hollow square Exited: the process is gone Each state has its own shape as well as its colour, so you can tell them apart without seeing colour, except that waiting and blocked share the triangle. A blocked pane counts as waiting everywhere waiting agents are counted (below). In the Team view the requests show under the agent's row. A permission asked by a terminal pane is answered in its drawer, where its terminal is, so its block has no Approve button; the buttons are for a question that offers choices and for a permission from a structured pane. A Down block offers "Ask the manager to reassign" only when the pane has a task. The number on a project in the rail counts panes that are waiting or blocked. The goal line and the goal tab count requests, so a pane with two requests is one in the rail and two there. A pane whose turn is over but that has background work still running, a command or subagent it started, is still Idle and its header says how many are "in background". Its dot is the working dot all the same, and its tooltip says it is working in the background. Such an agent is counted as working everywhere working agents are counted (below), though its own status stays idle. Hover the "in background" count to see what the work is, up to eight pieces: whether it is a shell command, a subagent, a monitor or something else, the description or command Claude Code gave for it, shortened, and how long ago Flockdeck first saw it. Text that looks like a secret (a token, a password given as a value) is hidden, with the same redaction the transcript recorder uses. A file path is shown as typed, though, even one to a secret file. The same text reaches the relay and phone views. A piece first seen only in the list Claude Code sends when a turn ends says "seen since", because it was already running by then. Where Claude Code gave nothing but an id, the list says "details unavailable (count only)" rather than guessing. Flockdeck keeps the list in memory only and never saves it. While an agent is idle with background work counted, Flockdeck checks that work against the conversation Claude Code has stored for the pane: 45 seconds after it goes idle, then less often while nothing changes. The first check reads the last 8 MB of the conversation, and later checks read only what has been added since. A piece is dropped only on evidence of its end, written after Flockdeck first saw the piece and after the last sign it was running: Claude Code's notice that the task completed or was stopped, a subagent's hand-back, a successful stop of the task, a subagent's own transcript ending on its hand-back, or a monitor running past the timeout it was started with, when Claude Code stops it. An older end in the history is about an earlier task and is ignored. For a short while afterwards the tooltip lists what ended and what showed it, under "Lately ended". A subagent whose transcript is still being written, or a command whose output file is still growing, counts as running. A piece with no sign of running for 30 minutes (no start, no end-of-turn list naming it, nothing being written) stays counted but is marked unverified, and the badge says so ( ◔ 1 in background, unverified). An idle agent whose background work is all unverified no longer counts as working, so its dot and its tab go back to idle. It still isn't treated as finished. There is no way to clear the count by hand. While a tool is running the pane header names it, so Read, Bash or Edit tells you what the agent is doing, not only that it is busy. Where else it shows The tab holding a waiting agent is marked ▲. A tab with an agent working, or idle between turns with background work still running (not counting work that is all unverified), has a pulsing filled dot instead; the ▲ takes its place when an agent there is waiting. The window title reports the count, ▲ 2 waiting while any agent is waiting, otherwise ● 3 working, so a waiting agent is visible in the taskbar with the window behind something else. The top bar counts the agents waiting and working across every open project, the same counts the window title draws from; an idle agent whose background work is still running counts as working, here and in the window title and the tab icon. Click the count for the same list Ctrl+Shift+A opens. The rail down the left of the window has a tile for each open project, and the tile says what that project's agents are doing, most urgent first: an amber badge where an agent is waiting on you, a pulsing cyan one where agents are working (one with background work still running counts) and none is waiting, and nothing where every pane is idle, exited, failed or not yet heard from, or there are no panes. So one that starts waiting in a project you are not looking at is seen from the one you are. Widen the rail and the count is written beside the name: ▲ 2 for two waiting, ● 3 for three working. The tile's tooltip and screen-reader name say it in words. A window reached through the relay shows the same. A desktop notification is raised when an agent blocks while the window is not in front, unless Desktop notifications is off in Settings › General. It is not raised when you are already looking at the window: the tab marker is enough, and a toast would be noise. Claude Code's own idle nudge (sent about a minute after a pane has simply gone quiet, waiting for a new prompt) never raises any of the above, for any pane: it says nothing more than that the pane is still there. A permission prompt or a real question always still reaches you, including for a helper another agent started for itself (see Agents and models). Ctrl+Shift+A lists every pane in every open project with its status, and jumps to any of them. Close finished panes clears out every agent pane that has gone idle and every pane that has exited cleanly, in every open project, in one go, like closing finished browser tabs. It asks nothing first, on purpose: a pane still waiting on you or still working is never touched, an idle shell is left alone, and one whose process failed (it never started, exited with an error, or was killed) is left alone too, since a failure is worth a look before it disappears. A pane locked with the padlock icon in its header, shut once locked, or Lock pane in the command palette is left open too, with a count of how many were skipped; a locked pane cannot be closed any other way either until you unlock it, though it can still be restarted. An idle agent that still has background work going (a command it started with run_in_background, or a background subagent) is not finished either, since closing it would kill that work. Its header says ◔ 1 in background while it has any, and so does its row in Ctrl+Shift+A. Flockdeck learns the work has ended when Claude Code tells the agent so, says at the end of a turn what is still running, or has recorded the end in the stored conversation (see above). Work that is counted but unverified still keeps the pane open. A Claude Code too old to say either keeps it counted until the agent stops it, the conversation is cleared, or the pane is closed by hand (or with flockdeck close -force). A background subagent calling tools after its agent's turn has ended leaves the pane idle, with that count and the working dot, rather than flickering between states for each call. A question or permission prompt it puts to you still turns it amber. Where it comes from For an agent that can report its own lifecycle, this is not screen scraping. Claude Code is launched with a generated --settings file registering its lifecycle hooks ( UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, Notification, Stop and the rest). Each event re-invokes this same binary in a hidden mode, and the report reaches the application over the loopback interface. Status therefore reflects what the agent is doing, not what its output happens to look like. Those settings are additive: your own settings, hooks and permissions still apply. Auto-approve read-only A pane can pass a plain read-only command ( git status, cat, grep) without stopping at Claude Code's permission prompt. It is off unless you turn it on, with the ✓ in the pane's header or in Settings. Anything that changes a file, or that it is not sure of, still asks. Auto-approve read-only has the policy and the settings. One answer is not reported by any event: a permission prompt answered from the keyboard. Enter turns the pane cyan, since allowing the tool starts it running. Refusing it puts Claude Code back at its prompt without a word, so a pane that is then heard from by nothing, neither an event nor anything it draws, for ten seconds goes back to grey. An agent that cannot report Not every coding agent has a lifecycle to report, and Flockdeck runs those too. For their panes the status is read from the terminal instead: the bell an agent rings when it wants you, a quiet timer for when it has stopped producing output, and, where its entry in agents.json gives it patterns, the lines it prints: the shape of a permission question, the shape of a prompt waiting to be typed at. Only the last few hundred bytes are looked at, with the escape sequences stripped, so a question two screens back does not keep a finished pane amber. That is a guess where the other is a fact, and it is worth knowing which you are looking at: Agents and models says which agents report and which are read. Where both exist, a reported event always wins. Letting Jev break the tie The one thing the terminal cannot tell is a pane that has gone quiet: finished, or stopped on a question. Flockdeck can ask TypeSafe's Jev model, a small model that answers a fixed multiple-choice question rather than writing anything. This sends terminal output to a third party, TypeSafe, which nothing else in Flockdeck does with what your panes print, so it is off by default and needs both of these: Settings › Status detection › Let TypeSafe's Jev help read pane status turned on. It can only be turned on from the machine itself, not from a window reached through the relay; turning it off works from a window reached through the relay too. A TypeSafe API key: either the one you paste into Settings › API keys › TypeSafe API key (kept on this machine with your other keys, never shown back, only ever sent to api.typesafe.ai, and only set from the machine itself), or TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the environment Flockdeck starts in. The one in Settings is used first. Saving a key does not turn anything on. With either missing, nothing is ever sent, and no error is shown. What is sent, when a pane of an agent that reports nothing has been quiet for a few seconds and its status is still a guess: the last 30 lines of its output, at most 2,000 bytes, with the escape sequences taken out and secrets redacted. It goes in one request holding that text and the two questions asked of it. The scrollback and the pane's name and folder are not sent. Before it is sent, the text goes through the redaction the transcript recorder uses, with additions for a terminal. The redaction takes out API keys of the common providers (Anthropic, OpenAI-style, GitHub, GitLab, AWS, Google, Slack, Stripe, Hugging Face, DigitalOcean, Twilio, npm), JWTs, bearer and basic credentials, passwords in URLs, private key blocks, and values assigned to a name such as TOKEN, SECRET or PASSWORD. The additions are these: any word that is a path to a secret file ( .env, id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials) is replaced, and so are three or more lines in a row of base64 (the body of a key whose first line has scrolled away). A key that the terminal wrapped onto the next line is joined first when the line before it is a full-width line, so it is caught in the common case. If nothing is left but redacted text, nothing is sent. Redaction works by pattern and does not catch every secret: a password or key with no recognisable shape, on a line that does not name it as one, is sent as it is on screen, and so is everything else in those lines (code, file names, prose). If a pane may show something you cannot send to a third party, leave this off. Shell panes, and agents that report their own status, are never sent. What it can change: a quiet pane called idle becomes waiting, or blocked, only when Jev answers with high confidence. It never turns waiting or blocked into anything else, and if it errors, is slow, is rate limited, or is unsure, the pane shows what it would have shown without it. Asks are limited to one per pane every 15 seconds, twelve per pane an hour and ten a minute in all, and the same output is not asked about twice in a row. After an error or a rate limit nothing is asked for a minute, and after a refused key or request for 15 minutes.

pages.title: Auto-approve read-only
pages.summary: Earlier versions called this auto-review. It has nothing to do with the diff review in Changes, which is where you read what an agent changed.
pages.text: Auto-approve read-only Earlier versions called this auto-review. It has nothing to do with the diff review in Changes, which is where you read what an agent changed. A pane can turn on Auto-approve read-only, which spares you the wait for some of what would otherwise stop and ask: the same hidden hook that reports a PreToolUse call can also carry a permission decision back, before Claude Code's own prompt ever opens, for a call Flockdeck is confident only reads. It works like Codex's auto_review, a reviewer looking at the request in front of it, but it never touches Claude Code's own permission settings and it can only ever say "let this one through," never "deny": off, or for a call it is not sure of, a pane behaves exactly as it always would. Today that reviewer is a fixed policy: a Bash call is let through only when it is a single call to a command that only ever reads ( git status, cat, grep and the like) inside the project, with nothing in it that could chain into something else or write anywhere; a call that changes a file, reads outside the project, or reads a secret file (a .env, a private key, a credentials file) is always left to ask. A git command is let through only when git itself, asked where the command will run, has nothing configured that would run a program or reach the network, and git status, git diff or git describe never in a repository with a submodule in it. A command too long to be judged whole is always left to ask. The details of that policy: The commands let through are a short list of ones that only read ( git status, git log, cat, grep and the like). A flag that makes one of them write or run something, such as git diff --output, sends the call back to ask. No go command is let through, because go env writes and any go command may download the toolchain go.mod names. A command over 4 KiB is asked about whatever it says, so it is never judged by its beginning alone. No argument may name a path outside the project: an absolute path, one under ~, or one that climbs out with ... Claude Code would have asked before reading there. The shell rewrites quotes, backslashes and globs before a command sees them, so a command holding any of those is asked about too. No argument may name a file whose contents are a secret in their own right: a .env file, a private key, an .npmrc, .netrc or .pgpass file, or a credentials file. A read of one would otherwise reach the transcript unseen. The public half of a key pair ( id_rsa.pub) is left alone. A git command is let through only once git itself, asked in the directory the command will run in, reports nothing configured that would run a program or reach the network: no core.fsmonitor command, external diff, textconv or filter driver (Git LFS's own is excepted), gpg program, trace2 target or partial-clone remote. That holds whether the setting comes from the repository, a file it includes, or your own global configuration. git status, git diff and git describe are asked about in any repository with a submodule in it, since each runs git again inside the submodule under that submodule's own configuration, which two ordinary files an agent writes into the project are enough to supply. Anything that changes a file ( Edit, Write, MultiEdit) is left to ask every time, on purpose. That is the kind of call a person is meant to see before it happens. These path checks read the command as text, not the filesystem. Auto-approve read-only is not a sandbox. A symlink inside the project that points outside it reads as an ordinary in-project name and is let through, and the secret-file check knows only conventional names. Both err towards reading, which is part of why it is off unless you turn it on, and why you should turn it on only for a pane whose agent you trust. It is off for a pane unless you turn it on, with the ✓ in the pane's header, or for new panes with Settings › General › Auto-approve read-only in new panes; a pane started from another one (a flockdeck spawn helper) starts as that pane is. A pane keeps its setting across restarts, whichever way you left it. Reading Flockdeck mail Reading Flockdeck mail is allowed in every pane, whether or not this switch is on, and it does not count towards the pane's auto-approved calls. Only these forms are allowed, written exactly so: flockdeck inbox, with -all and -json each at most once flockdeck inbox read <id>, with -json before the id if you want it, and an id of one to nine digits Anything else is asked about as usual: -wait, -follow, any other flag or extra word, sending a message ( flockdeck msg send), every other subcommand, a path to the program ( ./flockdeck), a variable set in front of it, a pipe, a quote, or a command over 4 KiB. It is also asked about when the folder the command runs in holds a file named flockdeck or starting with flockdeck. ( flockdeck.exe, flockdeck.ps1 and so on, in any letter case), since the shell could run that instead. A project that builds its own flockdeck binary into its root therefore never has mail reads allowed in that folder. The same goes when a flockdeck earlier on the pane's launch PATH than this application would run instead of it, when no flockdeck is found on the PATH at all, or when the PATH has a ~ entry. Words must be separated by single spaces. This works for agents that report their tool calls to Flockdeck (Claude Code). Other command-line agents have approval modes of their own, which Flockdeck does not change; their briefings say how to allow flockdeck inbox.

pages.title: Spend and limits
pages.summary: A pane's header says what its agent has spent in the conversation, and how close it is to the usage limit it runs under, so the agent that is burning money, or about to stop, can be picked out of a tab of six without asking each one.
pages.text: Spend and limits A pane's header says what its agent has spent in the conversation, and how close it is to the usage limit it runs under, so the agent that is burning money, or about to stop, can be picked out of a tab of six without asking each one. What the header shows Two small figures sit after the tool name, before the processor and memory figure: What it has spent. ~$1.24 is an estimate in US dollars. 84k tok is tokens read and written, shown where there is no price to put on them, such as a local model. Amounts from $1 have two decimal places, from a cent three, and below a cent four ( ~$0.0042). A + after the money, as in ~$0.400+, means some of the tokens had no price, so the figure is a floor. The tightest limit. 5h 72% means 72% of the five-hour window is used; 7d is the weekly one. A bar under it fills as the window does. It turns amber at 80% and red at 95%. Hover over either one for the rest: every window and when it resets, the tokens in, cached and out, and where the money figure came from. Nothing is shown for an agent that reports nothing. Today that is every agent except Claude Code. Every money figure is an estimate No figure here is your bill, and each one is written with ~ to say so. Claude Code works out its own session cost at list prices, and the header shows that figure, marked as Claude Code's own. It can differ from what you are charged: for example, a data-residency premium or a negotiated rate is not in it. Tokens are exact and carry no ~. On a Claude subscription If you use Claude Code on a Pro or Max plan, your money is fixed and what stops you is the usage window. So the header leads with the window, and shows tokens rather than dollars. The dollar figure goes in the tooltip, as what those tokens would have cost on the API. A limit belongs to your login, not to one pane. Every Claude pane on the same login shares the same five-hour and weekly windows, and so does claude.ai, and Claude Code on another machine. A reading from any pane is shown in all of them. Use elsewhere moves the window between readings, so a reading more than ten minutes old says when it was taken. How Claude Code's limits are read Claude Code hands its limits to one place only: the command that draws its status line, the line under its prompt. To read them, Flockdeck puts a small command of its own in that place for its panes. That command passes the figures to Flockdeck, then runs your own status line command with exactly the same input, and prints what yours prints. Your status line looks as it did. Where you have no status line of your own, doing this would cost you something: Claude Code hides most of the keyboard hints in its footer whenever any status line is set. So by default Flockdeck only does it where you already have a status line, and there it changes nothing you can see. To choose, open Settings › Agents & models › Claude Code's usage limits: Only where I have a status line is the default. Always shows the limits in every Claude pane. Where you have no status line of your own, the line under Claude's prompt is left empty and the footer hints go. Never leaves Claude Code's status line alone. The header then shows nothing for Claude panes. The choice applies to a pane when it starts. Use Restart pane from the command palette for one that is already running. Your own status line is looked up the way Claude Code looks for it: in the project's .claude/settings.local.json, then .claude/settings.json, then your own settings.json in Claude Code's folder. If you change it, restart the pane so the new command is used. The windows only appear for Pro and Max subscribers, and only after the first answer in a session. On an API key, a Claude pane shows its session cost instead. What stays on your machine Everything here is worked out on this computer, from what the agents themselves report. Flockdeck sends nothing about your spending anywhere, and makes no network request to find it out: no usage API, no price feed. If Flockdeck Remote is on, the figures travel with the rest of your panes' state to your own devices, through the relay, as the pane headers do. The figures are kept in memory only for now. They start again when a conversation does, with /clear or a new session, and when Flockdeck restarts.

pages.title: Rearranging what is already running
pages.summary: This page describes the old window. The current window shows a team as a graph and has no splitting, moving, tiling or merging of panes. Tabs can still be reordered, and every pane can be opened in the drawer.
pages.text: Rearranging what is already running This page describes the old window. The current window shows a team as a graph and has no splitting, moving, tiling or merging of panes. Tabs can still be reordered, and every pane can be opened in the drawer. A layout is rarely right first time. The agent you thought was a side errand turns out to be the one you are watching, and it is in the wrong corner. Nothing is started or stopped by moving it. A move relocates the pane in the layout tree, so the process, its conversation, its working directory and its scrollback all come along. The new arrangement is saved, so it comes back next time. Dragging a pane Drag a pane by its header. The pane under the pointer shows what would happen if you let go there: onto the left, right, top or bottom of another pane: it goes there, joining that row or column rather than nesting a new split inside it; onto the middle of another pane: the two exchange places, and the layout keeps its shape and proportions exactly as they were; onto another tab in the tab bar: it moves into that tab; onto the + button: it gets a tab of its own. Dragging a tab Where along another tab it lands decides what happens: onto the left or right end: it is reordered to there; onto the middle: the two tabs are merged, and one tab is left holding every pane of both. Each keeps the arrangement it had, and the room is shared out a column at a time rather than half to each tab: fold five tabs in one after another and you get five even columns, not one half the width and the rest squeezed into slivers you cannot grab a divider in; onto the + button: it goes to the end of the bar. A tab emptied by dragging its last pane away closes itself, and the pane is not closed with it. That is the difference between moving a pane out and closing it. Putting a tab back in order Every move here is relative (beside this pane, past that one), and enough of them leaves a tab with panes too narrow to grab a divider in or drop anything into. Tile these panes evenly is the way back: it lays the tab's panes out in rows of even columns, in the order they are already in, the same arrangement a team starts its agents in. From the keyboard Ctrl+Shift+←, Ctrl+Shift+→, Ctrl+Shift+↑ and Ctrl+Shift+↓ move the focused pane past its neighbour in that direction. The neighbour is chosen by what is on screen rather than by tree order, and where two panes are equally near, the upper or the left one is taken. The opposite arrow puts a move back, whatever the sizes of the panes it passed, as long as nothing else in the tab has moved since. The command palette carries the same moves, and Move pane to a tab of its own for the one dragging does by dropping a pane on +. It also has two that dragging cannot express as easily: Move this pane to tab: … and Merge tab into this one: … for every open tab, and Merge every tab into this one for when the agents you want to watch together are scattered across all of them. Move tab left and Move tab right move the tab on screen one place along the tab bar, as dragging it would. Merging is the reverse of dropping a pane on +: what one splits apart, the other gathers back up.
